opening.headline: When responses may contain inappropriate content or personal information, learn where filters are placed in the request/response path and who sets them.
body: Because LLM has a variety of uses, it can produce unexpected output. Answers or inaccurate content may be provided that do not match the brand tone, and personal information contained in the user's question may be revealed in the response. It is difficult to predict in advance what kind of output will be produced.

In this lesson, we'll explore how Google Cloud's Model Armor bidirectionally inspects prompts and responses. Next, we will check the principle that the filter is a classifier that produces confidence values ​​for each category and the threshold is the cutoff line, the exchange of false positives and false negatives, the difference between gateway-level filters and model-level safety settings, and the types of methods to de-identify sensitive information.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of Model Armor, Moderation, and safety settings
Explain that the filter is a classifier that produces a confidence value and the threshold is a decision line, and can distinguish between false positives and false negatives.
You can distinguish between gateway-level filters and model-level safety settings
It can explain why sensitive information risks occur on the output side and the types of de-identification methods.

screens.title: Responses may contain inappropriate content
screens.lead: Read on for three real-world examples we encounter when adding AI to our services. The point at which problems arise varies from case to case.

paragraphs: LLM is used for a variety of purposes, such as outlining questions, writing documents, and responding to consultations. As it has a wide range of uses, it may produce output that developers did not expect. Responses may contain offensive language or inaccuracies.

**Case 1. An answer that does not fit the brand tone.** In a service where polite response is the rule, the model answers with harsh expressions or inappropriate jokes. Even if there are no errors, trust in the service is shaken.

**Case 2. Response exposure of personal information.** The user wrote down a phone number or account number in the question, and the model repeats this in the response. When responses are passed to logs or other screens, sensitive information is spread.

**Case 3. Attempt to bypass prompt.** The user sends input attempting to unravel the service's safety rules. Failure to filter out the input stage can cause the model to produce responses that fall outside the rules.

All three cases have the same problem in that it is difficult to predict in advance what the output will be. So, we need a device to check the model's output and input outside of the app. The questions for this class are: Where is the filter placed in the request/response path, and who sets it?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Would all three problems above be solved if we just wrote down the prompts to respond kindly? Think again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let me think about whether I have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Think of a similar situation
screens.lead: If you think about each question on your own first and then choose, the instructor will organize it for you. You will not enter or submit your answers.

items.prompt: Have you ever seen a case where AI gave inappropriate answers or personal information was mixed in a service?
items.answer: These cases can often be seen in the news or shared within the company. Usually, it's not a case of a bad model, but rather a case where there's no device in place to filter the output before it reaches the user. This lesson focuses on where to place the device.

items.prompt: Have you ever experienced the inconvenience of normal sentences being blocked in a tool with content filters turned on?
items.answer: An overly strict filter blocks legitimate requests. This is a false positive. Conversely, missing a dangerous request is a false negative. That is why you need to choose the filter's sensitivity, not just turn it on. The following sections explore this in more detail.

items.prompt: Will the filter be on the model side or the app side?
items.answer: Both are possible. Specifying safety settings when calling a model filters it out at the model level, and putting a gateway in front of your app allows you to inspect requests and responses from all agents in batches. Depending on where it is filtered, who sets it and the scope of coverage will vary.

screens.outro: Now let's take a schematic look at where Model Armor fits into the request and response path.

screens.title: Where filtering enters the request/response path
screens.lead: Selecting the numbered markers in the picture will reveal what happens in each step. Note that Model Armor checks on both input and output.

visual.alt: Schematic of the request and response being checked twice between the app, Model Armor, and LLM.

markers.label: Receive prompt
markers.title: 1. The app receives a prompt
markers.body: The app receives the prompts entered by the user. Prompts at this point may contain personal information or circumvention attempts. The app configures this content to go through Model Armor rather than sending it directly to the model.

markers.label: Input check
markers.title: 2. Model Armor examines the prompt
markers.body: Model Armor scans the incoming prompts for sensitive or dangerous content. Prompt injection, harmful content, sensitive information, etc. are checked according to the filters and thresholds set in the template.

markers.label: Pass to model
markers.title: 3. Original or purified prompt goes to LLM
markers.body: If it passes the test, the original prompt will be passed on to the LLM, and if any sanitization has occurred to mask sensitive areas, the sanitized prompt will be passed on to the LLM. The model only sees input that has already been filtered out.

markers.label: response check
markers.title: 4. LLM creates and rechecks the response
markers.body: When LLM generates a response, Model Armor re-examines this response for potentially sensitive or dangerous content. Bidirectional testing is necessary because problems can occur in the output even if the input is clean. This structure of having guardrails on the input side and output side is common even if the products are different. Models that classify prompts and responses into a safety taxonomy, for example Llama Guard, are in the same place.

markers.label: Delivery of response
markers.title: 5. Cleansed response and filter details are returned
markers.body: The original or sanitized response is delivered to the user. At this time, Model Armor also sends details of the filters that worked and those that did not work in the response. Apps can use this information for logging or monitoring.

screens.outro: Now that we know that the test is bidirectional, let's look at the thresholds that determine how sensitive the filter will be.

ext.title: Inan et al., Llama Guard: LLM-based Input-Output Safeguard for Human-AI Conversations (2023)

screens.title: The filter provides confidence and the threshold determines
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to see which four results the filter determines. A filter is a classifier that produces a confidence value for each category for each request, and the threshold is a baseline that blocks anything above that number.

data.caption: Four outcomes of filter decisions and the impact of thresholds
columns: Requests that are actually in violation
rows: False positive: A legitimate request was incorrectly blocked. Users experience inconvenience.
Mitam: You missed a dangerous request. Dangerous content reaches the model or user.
Normal Pass: Normal request is processed as is.
It blocks even at lower confidence levels, reducing false negatives.
Even legitimate requests are prone to being caught, resulting in more false positives.
Since it is blocked only at high certainty, the number of false negatives increases.
Fewer legitimate requests result in fewer false positives.
data.notes: A single threshold cannot simultaneously reduce false positives and false negatives. It is a trade-off where reducing one side increases the other side. Also, since the classifier is a model, it can make incorrect decisions or be bypassed by clever inputs, so it is not assumed that a single filter prevents all risks. The safety classification system and certainty value, which contains which categories the classifier divides into which criteria, serves as the basis for the decision.

screens.outro: Based on this principle, let's see what happens in real settings when we move the threshold.

ext.title: Inan et al., Llama Guard: LLM-based Input-Output Safeguard for Human-AI Conversations (2023)

screens.title: Threshold: Trading confidence for false positives
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the threshold. The threshold determines what is filtered out and how much normal requests are blocked.

data.controlLabel: Threshold (how confident the filter will respond)

stops.body: It only filters out when the model has high confidence that the content is a violation. There are very few false positives that block legitimate requests, but low-certainty suspected violations do pass through. This setting is used in environments where user inconvenience must be minimized. Instead, violations with ambiguous judgments are not filtered out, so supplementation from other layers is necessary.

It is a balanced type that filters out content with a medium or high probability of violation. Both detections and false positives are at a reasonable level, making it a good default choice for general business apps.

We filter out violations even if the likelihood of a violation is determined to be low. Detections increase, but the risk of false positives increases. Still, in can't-miss categories like prompt injection and jailbreak, this setting is worth considering.

You can have separate templates for input and output. Because the risks in both directions are different. Attempts to circumvent the input are viewed more strictly, and leaks of sensitive information are viewed more stringently at the output.

The Gemini API also specifies harm categories and thresholds in pairs. Threshold names range from block_only_high to block_low_and_above, for example setting the hate_speech category to block_low_and_above will also block content that has a low probability of being hate speech. The concept is the same as Model Armor, except that the place of application is the model call. The same confidence standard is used, but the name and setting method are different for each service, so the values ​​for each service must be read separately.

screens.outro: The nature of the filter varies depending on where the threshold is set. Let's compare the two levels side by side.

screens.title: Gateway-level filters and model-level safety settings
screens.lead: Select the three tabs one by one to compare what changes depending on where the filter is placed.

tabs.label: gateway level
tabs.body:
**Agent Gateway** intercepts all prompts and responses to and from the agent and sends them to Model Armor. If Model Armor rolls ALLOW, it passes it to the agent; if it rolls BLOCK, the client receives an error and the request never reaches the agent. Responses are judged in the same way and either allowed or blocked altogether.

The advantage is that **the same security guidelines are applied consistently** without having to write filter code for each agent. You can use a single template for requests and responses in the Client-to-Agent direction, or have different templates for each direction. Templates can be configured to block or hide violations.

tabs.label: model level
tabs.body:
Safety filters in the Gemini API are adjusted **per-call** with safety_settings. This setting is intended to be adjusted during development to see if your app has more stringent or looser safety requirements. Adjust values ​​in only those categories as needed to match the risk level of your service.

However, core hazards, such as content that compromises child safety, cannot be moderated and will always be blocked. Model-level settings are determined by the code that calls the model, so values ​​may vary for each agent. The more teams you have, the bigger this gap becomes, risking different security standards.

tabs.label: Moderation
tabs.body:
OpenAI's Moderation is a tool that classifies the harmfulness of text and images and returns flags and numbers. The app decides how to use the numbers. You can filter content, send it to a review queue, or repeatedly take action on flagged accounts.

In other words, Moderation only provides a decision signal and does not determine the policy itself. You should not send any content known or suspected to be child sexual abuse to this API.

tabs.label: Compare at a glance
tabs.body:
**Who sets it?** The gateway level is set by the security organization as a template, and the model level is set by the calling developer.

**Where it applies.** The gateway applies to all agents governed by the gateway, and the model level applies to calls with settings.

**Consistency.** Gateway is high, model level can vary from call to call.

The two are not a substitution relationship, but rather overlapping layers.

screens.outro: Let's continue with the protection of sensitive information and safety guidelines that complement what the filter cannot prevent.

screens.title: Sensitive information protection and safety guidelines
screens.lead: Expand the items to see three elements that complement your filter.

items.title: Safety Instructions: Repeat the four steps
items.body: The process of creating a secure app is sequential. First, understand the risks your app poses, then **adjust mitigations** to reduce those risks, then **safety test** for your use case, and finally **feedback and monitor**. Adjustments and tests are repeated until the standard is reached. This means that rather than setting a threshold once and being done with it, you keep adjusting it while looking at the results.

items.title: Sensitive Data Protection(DLP)
items.body: Sensitive Data Protection is a service that **discovers, classifies, and de-identifies** sensitive data. Personally identifiable information (PII) or credentials entered at the LLM prompt can be screened and screened before being saved. Model Armor connects to this service's capabilities through sensitive information protection filters, which find and cleanse sensitive data from prompts and responses.

items.title: Why sensitive information is at risk on the output side
items.body: OWASP classifies sensitive information exposure as an independent risk for LLM applications. This is because personal information, financial information, health records, corporate secrets, and authentication credentials can be revealed through a model's responses. This information is output as output through the values ​​the user wrote in the question, the results of the searched document or tool, and what the model has learned. This is why the output must be inspected separately even if the input appears clean. There are three main principles of prevention: Mask (sanitize) sensitive values ​​before feeding them into the model, limit the scope of data the model touches to the least privileged, and look for patterns in the output to mask or erase them. Even if the product changes, these three judgment criteria remain the same.

items.title: Use of Moderation Results
items.body: The flags and numbers returned by Moderation are the ingredients of the policy. This signal allows apps to filter out content, send it for human review, or take action on repeat offender accounts. Which measures to take at which numbers must be determined based on the risk level of the service. It is important to note that the tool does not set the standards for you.

items.title: A filter is just one layer
items.body: Filters filter input and output to reduce exposure to or creation of dangerous content. However, filters do not prevent all problems and should be overlaid with permission restrictions, monitoring, and checks. For example, even if a response passes a filter, the actions that the agent can perform must be separately restricted, and what decision the filter made must be logged so that it can be reviewed later.

screens.outro: Now, let's look at examples of the types of transformations that de-identify sensitive information.

ext.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure

screens.title: Explanation: Types of Sensitive Information De-Identification Transformation
screens.lead: The instructor explains the transformations provided by Sensitive Data Protection one by one. Use the arrows to advance to the next transformation. Examples include phone number, age, and date.

steps.title: Redaction: Delete
steps.body: Delete all or part of detected sensitive values. This is a case where the account number space is left blank in the response. The original value cannot be restored, and although it is the simplest, its place in the sentence may appear empty. It is suitable for logs or reports that do not require values.

steps.title: Replacement: Change to another value
steps.body: Replaces the detected value with the specified replacement value. By changing the phone number to a designated symbol, such as [Phone Number], you can hide the value while maintaining the sentence structure. It is used when you want to hide only the value while leaving the information necessary for the model to understand the context.

steps.title: Masking: Covering a part
steps.body: Mask some characters in the value by replacing them with characters such as # or *. By covering the last digits of the number and leaving the first digits, it tells you what the value was like, but hides the actual value.

steps.title: Crypto-based tokenization: Encrypt with key
steps.body: Convert the original value to an encryption key. There are several types, some of which can be reversed to restore their original value. Unlike masking, the party with the key can restore the original value.

steps.title: Bucketing: generalizing to ranges
steps.body: Replace specific values with ranges of values. Instead of an exact age, change it to an age range, and instead of a specific temperature, change it to a range such as hot, normal, or cold. It can be used for analysis, but it makes it difficult to identify individuals. Dividing the intervals too finely reduces the effectiveness of generalization.

steps.title: Date shifting: Move the date
steps.body: Shift a sensitive date value by a random amount of time. Gaps between dates are maintained, allowing analysis of the sequence of events or elapsed time period, but not the actual dates. It is suitable for data where time order has meaning, such as medical treatment or orders.

screens.outro: Now that we know the types of transformations, let's look at layering multiple devices into one chatbot path.

screens.title: Commentary: Overlaying filters on chatbot paths
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of adding filters one by one to the customer service chatbot. Scroll through the steps with the arrows.

steps.title: Determine the input template
steps.body: The input template sets different thresholds for each category. For example, prompt injection and jailbreak detection are set to Low and above to ensure they are not missed, and the general harmful category is balanced to Medium and above.

steps.title: Sensitive information is masked and sent to the model.
steps.body: With Sensitive Data Protection, the phone number and account number written by the user are hidden and then sent to the model. If the model doesn't see the sensitive value, it can't iterate back in response. Masking at the input stage reduces risk before blocking at the output stage.

steps.title: Determine the output template
steps.body: Templates for output check that the model does not export sensitive information. This is because even if the input is clean, sensitive values ​​may appear in what the model learned or in the tool results. The output side threshold is set separately from the input side.

steps.title: Set model-level settings
steps.body: Model-level safety settings maintain defaults or adjust them depending on the domain of your service (e.g. children's education, medical consultation). Divide which floor is responsible for what to avoid overlapping gateway templates and roles. When the same category is tested at two levels with different criteria, it becomes difficult to know which setting determined the outcome.

steps.title: Look at the results and adjust again
steps.body: Monitor the filter details and logs returned by Model Armor and readjust the thresholds for categories with many false positives. This corresponds to the testing and monitoring phase of the safety instructions. After making adjustments, check again with the same log to see if false positives have actually been reduced.

screens.outro: Finally, we organize the entire class. A filter is not something you set up once and be done with; it is a device that you adjust by looking at the results.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Organizes the location of filtering, setting entity, threshold, and de-identification into one flow.

paragraphs: Model Armor is a service that bi-directionally inspects prompts and responses. Input is filtered before it reaches the model, and output is filtered before it reaches the user. Writing at the gateway level ensures that the same instructions are applied consistently to all agents, while model-level safety settings are adjusted by the caller for each model call.

The threshold is a confidence criterion. As you lower it, detections increase, but the number of false positives that block normal requests also increases. So, we decide differently depending on the category and direction, and continue to adjust by looking at the log.

Sensitive information can be de-identified through transformations such as deleting, replacing, masking, tokenizing, categorizing, and date shifting before sending it to the model. The answer to the first question, whether simply writing down friendly responses to the prompts is enough, is no. Prompts are just one layer, and you need to layer filters on the request and response paths. Remember this:

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Think about whether more sensitive information flows in your work - the request side or the response side - and think about what filters you want to put on that side. When one layer of the filter breaks through, it is good to also think about what the next layer is.

glossary.def: This is a Google Cloud service that inspects prompts and responses to filter out injections, harmful content, and sensitive information.
OpenAI's tool classifies the harmfulness of text and images and returns flags and numbers. It's up to the app to decide what to do with the results.
This value determines whether to block the content when there is a certain level of certainty that it is a violation.

A false positive is when a normal request is incorrectly blocked as a violation, and a false negative is when an actual violation is missed and passed. Lowering the threshold reduces false negatives and increases false positives.
It is a conduit that intercepts traffic to and from the agent and collectively applies controls such as Model Armor.
A Google Cloud service that discovers, classifies, and de-identifies sensitive data.

misconceptions.myth: Filters exist only within the model.
misconceptions.fact: Like a gateway, you can filter requests and responses outside of your model. Model-level settings and gateway-level filters are different layers.

misconceptions.myth: The lower the threshold, the safer it is.
misconceptions.fact: Lowering the threshold increases detections, but also increases false positives, blocking legitimate requests. It must be determined according to the category and direction.

misconceptions.myth: Masking and tokenization are the same thing.
misconceptions.fact: Masking involves covering some characters with other characters, while password-based tokenization encrypts with a key and may be reversible.

misconceptions.myth: Once set, classifier-based filters cannot be bypassed.
misconceptions.fact: The filter's classifier is also a model, so it can be bypassed by incorrect or clever input. So we overwrite it with permission restrictions, monitoring, and checking.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Filters are placed on both the request path and the response path.
The filter is a classifier that produces confidence values for each category, and the threshold is a cutoff line, so lowering the threshold reduces false negatives but increases false positives.
Gateway-level filters and model-level safety settings have different settings and scope of application.
Because the output also carries the risk of sensitive information, we combine input sanitization, data range limiting, and output inspection.
Sensitive information is de-identified and sent to the model through transformations such as sanitization, masking, and tokenization.
